title: Chapter XIII

teacherSummary.text: Mr. Bennet reads a letter from Mr. Collins, the clergyman cousin who will inherit Longbourn. Collins arrives, pompous and obsequious, praising his patroness Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

vocabulary.definition: (Law) To take by descent from an ancestor
vocabulary.context: Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inherit”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bennet, who assured him with some asperity that they were very well able to keep a good cook, and that her daughters had nothing to do in the kitchen.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “asperity”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An expression, by word or act, of approbation, regard, confidence, civility, or admiration
vocabulary.context: He had not been long seated before he complimented Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “compliment”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Though it is difficult,” said Jane, “to guess in what way he can mean to make us the atonement he thinks our due, the wish is certainly to his credit.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “atonement”: at- (Latin ad, "to") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I cannot be otherwise than concerned at being the means of injuring your amiable daughters, and beg leave to apologise for it, as well as to assure you of my readiness to make them every possible amends—but of this hereafter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “injure”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The art or process of preparing food for the table, by dressing, compounding, and the application of heat
vocabulary.context: The dinner too in its turn was highly admired; and he begged to know to which of his fair cousins, the excellence of its cookery was owing.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cookery”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “In point of composition,” said Mary, “his letter does not seem defective.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “defective”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + fect (Latin facere, "to make") + -ive (Latin -ivus, "tending to"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Collins was punctual to his time, and was received with great politeness by the whole family.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “punctual”: -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “There is some sense in what he says about the girls however; and if he is disposed to make them any amends, I shall not be the person to discourage him.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “discourage”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of seeing or beholding
vocabulary.context: Bennet’s heart, but for the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “view”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Clergymen often depended on wealthy patrons for their livings.

significance: Collins is a comic masterpiece who satirizes both sycophancy and the church's dependence on rank.
discussionQuestions: What words would you use for Collins's letter, and why?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

items.prompt: How does Mr. Bennet view the letter?
What tone does Austen use for Collins?
In the line “Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn.”, what does “inheriting” most nearly mean?
options: (Law) To take by descent from an ancestor
An expression, by word or act, of approbation, regard, confidence, civility, or admiration

answerKey.answer: (Law) To take by descent from an ancestor

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XIII,” how does Austen show an absurd cousin's letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XIII, how does Austen develop the idea of an absurd cousin's letter? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIII develops the idea of an absurd cousin's letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of an absurd cousin's letter. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XIII suggests about an absurd cousin's letter. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XIII to complicate the reader's understanding of an absurd cousin's letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of an absurd cousin's letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of an absurd cousin's letter follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XIII and its treatment of an absurd cousin's letter. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XIII as evidence for a larger claim about an absurd cousin's letter in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of an absurd cousin's letter. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “It certainly is a most iniquitous affair,” said Mr. Bennet, “and nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn. But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be a little softened by his manner of expressing himself.”

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What words would you use for Collins's letter, and why? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are inheriting, asperity, complimented, atonement, injuring. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn.” Webster's says: (Law) To take by descent from an ancestor. Now the word history: “inherit”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “asperity”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “compliment”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Clergymen often depended on wealthy patrons for their livings. Why does this chapter matter? Collins is a comic masterpiece who satirizes both sycophancy and the church's dependence on rank. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to an absurd cousin's letter.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “It certainly is a most iniquitous affair,” said Mr. Bennet, “and nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn. But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be a little softened by his manner of expressing himself.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XIII,” how does Austen show an absurd cousin's letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about an absurd cousin's letter, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes an absurd cousin's letter. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
